183.t: Henry Red Allen's imitation of Armstrong and why he did not rise
183.s: Watts and Alfred agree Red Allen was a fine player but copied Louis too closely, which they believe limited his reputation.
183.ch: Style, peers and the 1963 New Orleans scene
183.q: Yeah, yeah, yeah. And don't forget my little teacher now, Henry Red Allen.

183.t: Watts's own gut-bucket style apart from Armstrong
183.s: Watts says he took a few Armstrong licks but developed his own gut-bucket style, and made a name across Texas.
183.ch: Style, peers and the 1963 New Orleans scene
183.q: You know, I Lewis, if I'm playing a number, and I think about a couple of licks like Lewis would put in there. And if I want to, I put it in there. But I've got my own little gut bucket style. Yeah, most musicians do that. Like we used to work out in California. I used my own ideas, see.

641.t: Why New Orleans clarinetists had individual sounds
641.s: Barry asks why old New Orleans players had individuality while modern ones copy George Lewis; Joe says he never copied anyone.
641.q: Certainly nobody tried to play like Picou. Certainly I would never want to play like Picou. I would have maybe tried to copy a little bit with Picou, but I really never... Barry, I never tried to copy anybody.

641.t: Copyists today, and trumpet players imitating Louis
641.s: They discuss Michael White copying Johnny Dodds, trumpeters copying Louis, and Joe's self-described poor copying.
641.q: I know. Louis influenced so many of those guys. One thing about me, I never had a big desire to copy. I used to admire a lot of those guys; I liked what

240.t: Playing like Buddy Petit and Armstrong; Robichaux's advice to find his own style
240.s: He played fast runs and followed Armstrong note for note until old violinist Robichaux told him in 1930 to develop his own style.
240.q: all that. Buddy Pt, well, what I would say was a lot of, in those days they used to call it runs, we call them chords nowadays, you know, breaking chords, you know what I mean? Because you get to, in later years we studied those things and we actually properly, in other words, probably naturally…

42.t: Colyer's imitation of Bunk, and the lack of American records in England
42.s: Colyer copied records indiscriminately; American jazz was kept out of England at the time he left.
42.ch: Playing in New Orleans and influences
42.q: Yeah, well, the band was sort of meant to be like Bunk. See, George and Jim Crow both play in styles which I gather is fairly easy to imitate, even if not to, you know, to make it sound like the same, not have the same swing. And it's sort of basically simple stuff. I mean, it's much easier to copy…

878.t: Wiggs asks Harry about his own lyrical style
878.s: Wiggs praises Harry's lyrical, creative style and compares it to Bix; Harry cannot say where it came from and says it differs from Larry's.
878.q: I really can't, John. I just... I don't know. I guess it's just a style that came to me. As I said before, Larry was very creative. And maybe it's sort of ran the family, by the way I see.

911.t: Sweets Edison on originality and the saxophone lineage
911.s: Rowe quotes Harry Edison on being an originator rather than an imitator and asks how to find a sound after Coltrane.
911.q: Yeah. I can resonate with that.

668.t: Pee Wee Russell as an inimitable individualist
668.s: He says only Pee Wee could do Pee Wee and contrasts Armstrong's imitators who stayed individual with today's Clifford Brown clones.
668.q: He was very unique. Any time you want to hear somebody try to sound like him it’s laughable because you know who they’re doing. You know instantly they’re trying to mock — or not really mock but — if you’re trying to do Pee Wee, and I know somebody here who does him very well, but at the same time…

584.t: Sweets Edison on originality and recognizable sound
584.s: Rowe quotes Sweets Edison on being an originator rather than an imitator.
584.ch: Sideman career and finding a sound

120.t: Discouragement, the Depression, and refusing to copy Bix or Louis
120.s: He stuck with music for love of playing, took only a few notes from Bix and Armstrong, and condemns Red Nichols copying Bix note for note.
120.ch: Looking back and the lean years
120.q: All right - so I was a little. Maybe a little but I never could play like they do because I was too damn dumb to copy anybody, but I thought if I got a few notes that sounded like Louie that was enough and I used to play kind of Bix ; I remember once a record came up where they thought I was Bix on…
